routes.label: Magnitudes and a forced final factor

officialSolution.label: 2017 AMC 12A

question: The vertices \(V\) of a centrally symmetric hexagon in the complex plane are given by \[ V=\left\{\begin{gathered} \sqrt2 i,\;-\sqrt2 i, \\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt8}(1+i), \\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt8}(-1+i), \\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt8}(1-i), \\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt8}(-1-i) \end{gathered}\right\}. \] For each \(j,\) \(1\le j\le12,\) an element \(z_j\) is chosen from \(V\) at random, independently of the other choices. Let \(P=\prod_{j=1}^{12}z_j\) be the product of the \(12\) numbers selected. What is the probability that \(P=-1?\)
solution:
First match the magnitude of the product to \(|-1|=1\). Put
\[
A=\{\sqrt2 i,-\sqrt2 i\},\qquad B=V\setminus A.
\]
Each element of \(A\) has magnitude \(\sqrt2\), while each element of \(B\) has magnitude
\[
\sqrt{\frac{1^2+1^2}{8}}=\frac12.
\]
If exactly \(k\) of the twelve factors belong to \(A\), then
\[
|P|=(\sqrt2)^k\left(\frac12\right)^{12-k}
=2^{3k/2-12}.
\]
This equals \(1\) exactly when \(k=8\). Thus every successful selection has eight factors from \(A\) and four from \(B\).

The eight factors from \(A\) multiply to \(\pm16\), since \((\sqrt2)^8=16\) and \(i^8=1\). To track the other four factors, set \(u=(1+i)/\sqrt8\). Then
\[
B=\{u,iu,-u,-iu\},\qquad
u^2=\frac{i}{4},\qquad u^4=-\frac1{16}.
\]
A product of four elements of \(B\) therefore has the form \(u^4i^m\) for an integer \(m\). Combining this with the product from \(A\), the possible values of \(P\) are \(1,i,-1,-i\).

Fix the eight \(A\)-values and the first three \(B\)-values, reading the \(B\)-positions in increasing index order. As the fourth \(B\)-value runs through \(u,iu,-u,-iu\), the resulting products differ by the factors \(1,i,-1,-i\). They attain the four possible values exactly once, so exactly one choice makes \(P=-1\).

There are \(\binom{12}{4}\) choices for the four \(B\)-positions. For each such pattern, the eight \(A\)-entries have \(2^8\) choices and the first three \(B\)-entries have \(4^3\) choices; the remaining entry is forced. Every successful ordered selection is counted once because its four \(B\)-positions are uniquely determined.

All \(6^{12}\) ordered selections are equally likely, so
\[
\Pr(P=-1)
=\frac{\binom{12}{4}\,2^8\,4^3}{6^{12}}
=\frac{495\cdot4}{3^{12}}
=\boxed{\frac{2^2\cdot5\cdot11}{3^{10}}}.
\]
The answer is choice E.
